name: Ho Chi Minh City
tagline: French colonial relics meet frenetic, neon-lit energy.
bestMonths: Jan, Feb, Mar, Nov and Dec
whenBlurb: Come December to April for dry, bright days; time it with Tet in February for the city at its most festive, and brace for daily downpours from May to October.

ourTake.lede: Saigon rewards appetite and energy more than sightseeing, the War Remnants Museum and the Reunification Palace are worth a serious half-day, but the city's real pleasure is at the table and on the street after dark. Base yourself in District 1 for a first visit, then cross into District 3 or Binh Thanh for the food locals actually queue for. Don't try to see it from a bus; the heat and the traffic mean the best moves are short, deliberate, and broken up by a good rooftop.
ourTake.comeIf: You want energy, history and superb food, with the Mekong Delta within easy reach.
ourTake.skipIf: You want calm and space; the city is fast, dense and relentless in its traffic.

heading.text: Ho Chi Minh City, in hand.

guide.lede: Where to stay, what to do, where to eat, and where the night goes, grouped by price, every address earned by a name worth trusting.

items.name: The Reverie Saigon
credentials: The Leading Hotels of the World, the sole Vietnamese member
MICHELIN Guide Hotel (Ho Chi Minh City selection)
items.description: Vietnam's most extravagant address, a maximalist Italian-designed palace of marble, gilt and glass atop the Times Square tower.

items.name: Park Hyatt Saigon
items.area: District 1 (Đồng Khởi), opposite the Opera House
credentials: MICHELIN Guide Hotel (Ho Chi Minh City selection)
items.description: French-colonial calm on Lam Son Square, the city's most quietly assured luxury house, facing the Opera House.

items.name: Hôtel des Arts Saigon, MGallery
credentials: MICHELIN Guide Hotel (Ho Chi Minh City selection)
World Travel Awards, Leading Lifestyle Hotel in Asia
items.description: A 1930s Indochine dream, Art Deco interiors, a museum's worth of period art, and a glorious rooftop pool over the city.

items.name: Caravelle Saigon
credentials: MICHELIN Guide Hotel (Ho Chi Minh City selection)
items.description: The war-correspondents' hotel since 1959, a genuine piece of Saigon history on Lam Son Square, with the legendary Saigon Saigon rooftop bar.

items.name: Hotel Majestic Saigon
credentials: MICHELIN Guide Hotel (Ho Chi Minh City selection)
items.description: Parisian opulence on a bend of the Saigon River since 1925, stained glass, chandeliers and a river-facing rooftop, the city's oldest grande dame.

items.name: The Myst Dong Khoi
credentials: MICHELIN Guide Hotel (Ho Chi Minh City selection)
items.description: A design-forward boutique that celebrates old Saigon, greenery, craft and a rooftop pool tucked just off Đồng Khởi.

items.name: Sofitel Saigon Plaza
credentials: MICHELIN Guide Hotel (Ho Chi Minh City selection)
items.description: A polished, well-placed French luxury tower on leafy Lê Duẩn, dependable service and a rooftop pool.

items.name: Renaissance Riverside Hotel Saigon
credentials: MICHELIN Guide Hotel (Ho Chi Minh City selection)
items.description: A well-run riverside tower with wide Saigon River views and a top-floor pool, comfortable and central.

items.name: Reunification Palace (Independence Palace)
items.description: The 1960s modernist presidential palace whose gates a North Vietnamese tank crashed through on 30 April 1975, ending the war. Inside it is frozen in that decade: the president's office, the war-room maps, the rooftop helipad, and the eerie basement bunker of telex machines. A private guide makes the political geography legible for a multi-generation family, and the leafy grounds give the grandparents somewhere shaded to pause.

items.name: War Remnants Museum
items.description: The city's most affecting museum, telling the war from the Vietnamese side through photography, captured aircraft and tanks in the courtyard, and unflinching galleries on Agent Orange. It is emotionally heavy and best approached with older children rather than the very young; a guide who can pace the visit and step outside when needed is worth arranging.

items.name: Saigon Central Post Office
items.description: A gloriously preserved 1890s beaux-arts hall often attributed to the Gustave Eiffel era, with a vaulted iron-and-glass ceiling, antique wall maps of old Cochinchina, and a huge portrait of Ho Chi Minh at the far end. Still a working post office, so you can send a postcard from the very desks; five minutes on foot from the cathedral.

items.name: Notre-Dame Cathedral Basilica of Saigon
items.description: The twin red-brick spires facing the post office are the postcard image of colonial Saigon, built with materials shipped from France. A major restoration runs to around 2027, so the interior is closed to visitors and the towers are under scaffolding; admire and photograph the exterior only, and note Masses still continue for worshippers.

items.name: Saigon Opera House (Municipal Theatre)
items.description: A jewel-box 1900 French opera house on Lam Son Square, its ornate facade flanked by the Continental and Caravelle hotels. The interior is best seen by booking the resident A O Show, a bamboo-and-acrobatics spectacle that tells rural Vietnamese life without a word of dialogue, making it an easy, elegant multi-generational evening.

items.name: Nguyen Hue Walking Street & People's Committee
items.description: A broad pedestrian boulevard running from the ochre, French-baroque People's Committee building (city hall, floodlit and photogenic at night, exterior only) down to the river, with a statue of Ho Chi Minh at the head. It comes alive in the cool of the evening with families, buskers and fountains; the natural place for a post-dinner stroll.

items.name: The Cafe Apartment (42 Nguyen Hue)
items.description: A nine-storey 1960s residential block on the walking street, every balcony now a different independent cafe, boutique or gallery, its facade a mosaic of signboards and fairy lights. Ride the tiny paid lift to the top and work your way down; a fashionable, very Instagrammable stop for younger travellers with a coffee at each landing.

items.name: Bitexco Financial Tower Saigon Skydeck
items.description: The helipad-crowned lotus-bud tower that defined the skyline before Landmark 81; its 49th-floor Skydeck gives a compact, central 360-degree view over the river bend and the colonial core. Being downtown, it is the easiest sunset viewpoint to fold into a District 1 afternoon, and the cafe-bar floors let the family linger over the lights coming on.

items.name: Landmark 81 SkyView
items.description: Vietnam's tallest building at 461 metres, its bamboo-bundle silhouette rising over a riverside park. The observation floors near the summit deliver the highest view in the country, with a glass-edge deck and cafe; pair it with a walk in the landscaped park below. A driver is sensible as it sits across the river from the tourist core.

items.name: Ben Thanh Market
items.description: The clock-towered 1914 covered market at the heart of downtown, a dense warren of fabric, lacquerware, coffee, dried fruit and souvenir stalls where haggling is expected. Best in the cooler morning for the food aisles; a guide or driver keeps a large group together and steers you to the fixed-price textile and lacquer stalls for cleaner buying.

items.name: Museum of Vietnamese History (History Museum)
items.description: An elegant 1929 Indochinese-style pavilion inside the Botanical Gardens, holding Cham sculpture, Oc Eo antiquities, a preserved mummy and dynastic bronzes. Compact and calm, it pairs naturally with the neighbouring zoo and gardens for a family morning, and offers real depth on the civilisations that preceded French Saigon.

items.name: Fine Arts Museum (Bao Tang My Thuat)
items.description: A honey-coloured 1930s mansion of a wealthy Chinese merchant, complete with the city's oldest lift and stained glass, now hung with lacquer paintings, silk works and wartime art. As much a house-museum as a gallery, it is a quieter, more architectural stop for those who have had their fill of temples and markets.

items.name: Ho Chi Minh City Museum (Gia Long Palace)
items.description: A grand neoclassical 1885 palace, once a governor's residence and later a presidential refuge, its bunker tunnels still beneath. Galleries trace Saigon's social history, and its gardens are a favourite for local wedding photography. A short, air-conditioned counterpoint a block from the cathedral and post office.

items.name: Jade Emperor Pagoda (Chua Ngoc Hoang)
items.description: The most atmospheric Taoist temple in the city, built by the Cantonese community in 1909, thick with incense, carved wooden deities and a hall of the twelve midwives where couples pray for children. Small, dim and intensely alive; go early morning, dress with shoulders and knees covered, and let a guide unpack the crowded symbolism. Admission is free.

items.name: Thien Hau Temple
items.description: The finest of Saigon's Chinese temples, dedicated to Mazu the sea goddess, its courtyard hung with vast spirals of coiled incense smoke and its roofline crowded with intricate ceramic figurines. The spiritual heart of Chinatown and a photographer's temple; combine with a wander through Cholon's old shophouse lanes.

items.name: Binh Tay Market & Cholon (Chinatown)
items.description: The grand yellow, pagoda-roofed wholesale market anchoring Cholon, Saigon's centuries-old Chinese quarter of herbalists, temples and gold shops. Less polished and more working than Ben Thanh, it rewards the curious traveller who wants the city's trading soul; a driver makes the run out from District 1 painless.

items.name: Saigon River dinner cruise
items.area: Saigon River (boarding Bach Dang Pier / Nha Rong)
items.description: An evening on the water with a buffet and live music as the illuminated Bitexco and Landmark 81 slide past; a relaxed, low-effort way to end a day for a group of mixed ages. Private charters can arrange a proper set menu with vegetarian courses on request rather than the standard buffet.

items.name: Cu Chi Tunnels
items.description: The vast network of hand-dug Viet Cong tunnels where families lived, cooked and fought underground; you can crawl a widened, lit section and see the camouflaged trap doors and living quarters. A powerful half-day for older children and history-minded travellers; a private car and guide beat the packed group buses, and the Ben Duoc entrance is quieter than Ben Dinh.

items.name: Cao Dai Holy See, Tay Ninh
items.description: The dazzling cathedral of Caodaism, Vietnam's home-grown faith blending Buddhism, Catholicism, Taoism and more, its nave a riot of dragon-wrapped pillars and a divine all-seeing eye. Time the visit for the noon ceremony, when white-, yellow- and blue-robed adherents fill the hall in silent ranks; galleries above let visitors watch respectfully. Often paired with Cu Chi or Ba Den.

items.name: Ba Den Mountain (Black Virgin Mountain)
items.description: The highest peak in southern Vietnam, capped by a hilltop temple complex and reached by a record-holding cable car that spares the climb. The summit views over the Tay Ninh plain and the giant Buddha statues make it an easy, spectacular add-on to the Cao Dai temple for grandparents and children alike.

items.name: Mekong Delta day trip (My Tho & Ben Tre)
items.description: The classic taste of the delta: a boat out onto the wide brown river to the islands, a sampan glide through palm-shaded canals, and stops for coconut candy, tropical fruit and honey tea. The nearest and easiest delta escape from the city; a private boat avoids the tour-group crush and lets a family set its own gentle pace.

items.name: Cai Rang floating market & Can Tho
items.area: Mekong Delta (Can Tho, ~3.5-4 hours south; overnight recommended)
items.description: The delta's largest floating market, where wholesalers hoist samples of produce on tall poles above their laden boats at dawn. Because it peaks early, it rewards an overnight in Can Tho and a pre-sunrise boat; the real, working delta rather than the day-tripper version, best done unhurried with a private guide.

items.name: Vung Tau seaside
items.area: Vung Tau (day trip / weekend, ~2 hours southeast)
items.description: The nearest coast to Saigon, a headland town of colonial villas, a hilltop Christ statue you can climb inside for sweeping sea views, and lighthouse lanes. An easy weekend breather from the city heat; historically reached by hydrofoil, though a private car is now the simplest door-to-door option.

items.name: Con Dao Islands
items.area: Con Dao archipelago (far; ~45-min flight from HCMC)
items.description: A remote, protected archipelago of empty beaches, coral reefs and turtle nesting, layered with the sombre history of its former French and American political prisons. The most exclusive escape in reach of Saigon, home to a landmark barefoot-luxury resort; fly in for a few nights of privacy, diving and reflection rather than a day trip.

items.name: District 3 & the villa quarter
items.description: The leafiest slice of central Saigon, of tamarind-lined boulevards, French villas, the pink Tan Dinh Church and quiet specialty cafes. A neighbourhood for a slow guided walk rather than a checklist of sights, giving a sense of how the city's professional and old-money families actually live.

items.name: Vietnamese coffee culture
items.description: Coffee is Saigon's daily ritual, from robusta dripped over condensed milk (ca phe sua da) to the whipped egg coffee and the modern coconut-coffee. Time is well spent letting a guide take you from a plastic-stool pavement stall to a hidden third-wave roaster; it is one of the most authentic and effortless ways into local life for the whole family.

items.name: Banh mi & street-food trail
items.description: Saigon's street kitchen is among Asia's finest: the crackling French-Vietnamese banh mi, pho, broken-rice com tam and the fresh spring rolls of the south. A vetted evening food walk with a private guide can be routed to clean, trusted vendors and briefed in advance for vegetarian and Jain-friendly options, turning a daunting street scene into a highlight.

items.name: Bui Vien Walking Street
items.description: The city's loud, neon backpacker strip, a river of bars, street barbecue and music after dark. Not a luxury experience but a genuine slice of the city's nightlife energy, best sampled briefly and early from a quiet rooftop above the fray rather than in the thick of the crowd.

items.name: Tao Dan Park & the bird-cafe scene
items.description: A shaded downtown park where, in the early morning, locals bring caged songbirds to a corner cafe to sing together, alongside tai chi and badminton. A charming, free window into everyday Saigon life for early risers, a few minutes from the Reunification Palace.

items.name: Xu Hoai / Ao Dai & lacquer artisan visits
items.description: Saigon is the place to have a silk ao dai tailored within a day or two and to see traditional son mai lacquerware being layered and polished in small workshops. A private introduction to a trusted tailor or atelier turns shopping into a genuine craft experience and a lasting souvenir for the family.

items.name: Rooftop bars over the city
items.description: Saigon does the sky-high sundowner beautifully, from long-running perches above Lam Son Square to sleek towers over the river. An elegant, air-conditioned way to watch the chaos of the streets resolve into a glittering skyline; the natural apertif before a river-view dinner.

items.name: Fine dining & the modern-Vietnamese table
items.description: The city now carries a serious high-end dining scene, from refined takes on regional Vietnamese cooking to internationally recognised tables. Worth booking ahead through a concierge, and easy to brief for vegetarian tasting menus; the leafy expat quarter of Thao Dien adds a relaxed, garden-restaurant option across the river.

items.name: The colonial grand hotels (Continental, Majestic, Rex)
items.description: A trio of legends: the Continental of Graham Greene's Quiet American, the riverfront art-deco Majestic, and the Rex with its wartime rooftop garden bar where correspondents once gathered. Even non-guests can take afternoon tea or a rooftop drink and step straight into old Saigon's story.

items.name: Mariamman Hindu Temple
items.description: A vivid South-Indian temple to the goddess Mariamman, its gopuram crowded with painted deities, tucked among the downtown shophouses. For an Indian family it is a familiar and welcoming pause amid a very foreign city, and a reminder of Saigon's old Tamil trading community; a short walk from Ben Thanh Market.

items.name: Vinh Nghiem Pagoda
items.description: One of the largest Buddhist pagodas in the city, its Japanese-influenced multi-storey tower and serene halls a calm counterpoint to the Chinese temples of Cholon. Spacious and uncrowded, it is an easy, dignified stop for a family and especially atmospheric around the lunar festivals.

items.name: Southern Women's Museum
items.description: An unexpectedly moving museum devoted to the women of southern Vietnam, their traditional dress, and their extraordinary role in the war. Small, well presented and rarely busy, it adds a human and gendered dimension to the harder-edged war narrative of the bigger museums.

items.name: Turtle Lake (Ho Con Rua)
items.description: A landmark 1960s concrete lotus-and-water roundabout that has become a beloved evening hangout for young Saigon, ringed by street-snack carts. Not a monument so much as a mood, best experienced at dusk with a fresh coconut or a plate of banh trang tron among the students.

items.name: Botanical Gardens & Saigon Zoo
items.description: One of the oldest zoos and botanical gardens in the world, a shaded green lung beside the History Museum with mature rain trees and orchid houses. A gentle option for families with younger children needing a break from museums and traffic, right in the centre of District 1.

items.name: Tan Dinh Church (the Pink Church)
items.description: A candy-pink, Romanesque-Gothic Catholic church from the 1870s that has become one of the city's most photographed facades. A quick, cheerful stop while exploring District 3, and a chance to see a working parish church while the more famous cathedral remains under restoration.

items.name: Independence-era street art & the Post-Office lane cafes
items.description: The lanes and hidden apartment-block cafes around the cathedral and post office hide a low-key creative scene of galleries, design shops and vintage stores. Worth an unhurried wander with a guide who knows which doorways open onto courtyards, for travellers who prefer texture over headline sights.

items.name: Local morning market & pho breakfast
items.description: Beyond the tourist markets, the neighbourhood wet markets at dawn are where the city really shops, and the surrounding stalls serve the day's best pho. A private early walk here, followed by breakfast at a decades-old pho counter, is one of the most rewarding and grounding experiences the city offers.

items.name: Ănăn Saigon
items.area: District 1, Ton That Dam / old market lanes
items.description: Vietnam's first Michelin star, chef Peter Cường Franklin reimagines street food as fine dining, most famously his caviar-topped bánh mì.

items.name: Akuna
items.description: Creative European cooking with Vietnamese soul from an Australian-trained chef, the city's most exciting new tasting menu.

items.name: Hibana by Koki
items.area: District 1 (Đồng Khởi), Hôtel des Arts Saigon
items.description: An intimate teppanyaki counter of Japanese precision and premium produce, one of the hardest seats in Saigon.

items.name: The Royal Pavilion
items.area: District 1 (Đồng Khởi), Hôtel des Arts Saigon
items.description: Refined Cantonese with a heritage dim sum lunch, the most polished Chinese kitchen in the city, inside Hôtel des Arts.

items.name: Tầm Vị
items.description: Vietnamese home cooking kept exact and unhurried, the family recipes of the south and centre, raised to a star.

items.name: Quince Saigon
items.description: Wood-fire, market-led cooking from a well-travelled kitchen, bright, generous plates and a buzzy room.

items.name: Nhau Nhau
items.description: A modern Vietnamese 'drinking-food' bar, bold, snacky, cocktail-driven cooking that landed on the regional radar fast.

items.name: Cục Gạch Quán
items.description: Homestyle Vietnamese cooking in a restored old villa full of antiques, rustic, romantic and much-loved.

items.name: Hum Vegetarian
credentials: Widely regarded as the city's leading vegetarian restaurant, a fixture on Saigon dining guides
items.description: Refined, fully plant-based Vietnamese cooking in a calm garden setting, meat-free without compromise.

items.name: Phở Hòa Pasteur
items.description: One of Saigon's most storied phở houses, a generous southern bowl piled with herbs, since decades back.

items.name: Phở Phượng
items.description: A single, perfect southern phở, clean broth, tender beef, no ceremony.

items.name: Phở Minh
items.description: Beef noodle soup from a tucked-away alley since 1945, and a famous flaky pâté chaud pastry alongside.

items.name: Cơm Tấm Ba Ghiền
items.description: The city's most famous broken-rice plate, an outsized grilled pork chop over rice, exactly as Saigon likes it.

items.name: Bún Bò Huế 14B
items.description: A tiny stall serving one of the city's best bún bò Huế, the spicy, lemongrass-rich beef noodle soup of central Vietnam.

items.name: Bánh Mì Huỳnh Hoa
items.description: Saigon's most famous bánh mì, a fully loaded cold-cuts-and-pâté baguette that draws a permanent queue.

items.name: Saigon Saigon Rooftop Bar, Caravelle
credentials: Inside the historic Caravelle Saigon, a MICHELIN Guide Hotel and genuine Saigon landmark
items.description: The war-correspondents' rooftop since 1959, live music and a wraparound view over Lam Son Square and the Opera House.

items.name: Stir
credentials: Asia's 50 Best Bars 2025 (No. 61), Vietnam's highest-placed bar
items.description: Saigon's most celebrated cocktail bar, a hidden first-floor room reworking Vietnam's street drinks into precise, low-key cocktails.

items.name: Drinking & Healing
items.description: Industrial-chic and inventive, cocktails built on local herbs and ingredients on the second floor of an old apartment block.

items.name: Layla, Eatery & Bar
credentials: Asia's 50 Best Discovery (Ho Chi Minh City)
items.description: Artful cocktails and chilled vibes in a shabby-chic old colonial apartment, Summer Experiment's cooler big sister.

items.name: Summer Experiment
credentials: Asia's 50 Best Discovery (Ho Chi Minh City)
items.description: A playful, experimental cocktail den hidden in the same colonial block as Layla, one of Saigon's cult drinking rooms.

items.name: Social Club Rooftop Bar, Hôtel des Arts
credentials: Atop the MICHELIN-listed, MGallery Hôtel des Arts Saigon
items.description: An infinity pool and one of the highest, most stylish rooftops in town, the District 3 skyline laid out below.

items.name: Chill Skybar
credentials: Ho Chi Minh City's landmark rooftop skybar, a long-standing fixture of the night scene
items.description: The city's original see-and-be-seen skybar, an open-air deck high over District 1 with a full skyline sweep.

items.name: Blank Lounge, Landmark 81
credentials: Atop Landmark 81, the tallest building in Vietnam, the city's highest bar-lounge
items.description: Drinks near the top of Vietnam's tallest tower, the highest, most panoramic perch over the whole city and the Saigon River.

plan.heading: 3 days in Ho Chi Minh City, done well
plan.lede: A day-by-day shape for the trip, the pace we would set. Your advisor books the flights and the rooms; the days are yours.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: Base yourself at The Reverie Saigon, then walk District 1, the Central Post Office, Notre-Dame, the Opera House, before the heat.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: The War Remnants Museum, unhurried and sobering, then coffee at L'Usine on Le Loi.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Dinner at Anan Saigon, chef Peter Cuong Franklin's Michelin-starred street food reimagined; drinks upstairs at Nhau Nhau.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: Explore Cholon, the old Chinese quarter, the Thien Hau Temple and the Binh Tay market's morning trade.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: A private sampan on the Saigon River, then afternoon tea at the Hotel Continental, Graham Greene's old haunt.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Stella Michelin dining at Nen (relocated tasting menu) or a refined table at The Reverie's R&J; late drinks at Layla.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: Early departure by private car to the Cu Chi tunnels, walked with a historian rather than a tour guide.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: Return for lunch, then the Jade Emperor Pagoda and a slow browse of the antique dealers on Le Cong Kieu.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Rooftop aperitif at the Social Club, then dinner at Michelin-listed Esta by Francis Thuan Do.

items.name: District 1 (Dong Khoi)
items.description: The polished centre, grand hotels, the opera house and the main sights within walking distance; the natural first-visit base.

items.name: District 3
items.description: Leafier and more residential, with villa cafes and serious local restaurants, for repeat visitors who want the everyday city.

items.name: Thao Dien (District 2)
items.description: Riverside, green and international, with a relaxed expat scene, better for longer, quieter stays away from the centre's intensity.

events.name: Tet (Lunar New Year)
events.note: Nguyen Hue walking street becomes a vast flower festival; the city glows but many kitchens and shops close for the holiday.

events.name: Reunification Day
events.note: Marks the end of the war in 1975 with parades and fireworks, and is felt most sharply in the city where it happened.

events.name: Mid-Autumn Festival
events.note: Cho Lon's Chinatown lights up with lanterns, lion dances and mooncake stalls in the city's most atmospheric quarter.

onGround.heading: On the ground
onGround.note: Stay in District 1 near the Opera House or Dong Khoi for proximity to dining and heritage; the city is hot and humid year-round, and reservations at the best rooftop and speakeasy venues are worth arranging in advance.

rows.label: Arriving
rows.value: Fly into Tan Son Nhat International (SGN); a private car with fast-track handling brings you the short 20-to-30-minute distance into District 1.

rows.label: Getting around
rows.value: A private driver is the sensible default given the motorbike density; District 1's core is walkable in the cooler evening hours.

rows.label: Connectivity
rows.value: eSIM (Viettel) or airport SIM gives strong 4G/5G everywhere; wifi is reliable across hotels and cafes.

rows.label: Money
rows.value: Vietnamese dong (VND); cards work widely in District 1, keep some cash for street food and markets, and tipping is a small optional gesture.

rows.label: Climate
rows.value: December to April is the dry window, December to February is coolest and driest, ideal. May to November is the wet season: reliable heavy afternoon downpours for a few hours, then it clears, so it is manageable but humid.

rows.label: Flights from India
rows.value: Direct from Delhi in about 5h30m on Air India (daily), Vietnam Airlines and Vietjet into Tan Son Nhat (SGN); Mumbai has some direct service, Bengaluru typically connects. Air India's daily frequency gives the most flexible business-class option; the airport is close to District 1, so a car transfer is 20-30 minutes.

rows.label: Health & safety
rows.value: No mandatory vaccinations from India; hepatitis A and typhoid advised. The city is safe but has Southeast Asia's most persistent motorbike bag-snatching, keep phones and bags away from the roadside. Bottled water only.

rows.label: Dining, veg & Jain
rows.value: Strong vegetarian scene, again helped by Buddhist 'chay' restaurants where Jain-friendly requests (no onion/garlic) are understood. Indian dining is well-established in this larger city, Ganesh and Baba's Kitchen are dependable for North and South Indian.
